_comment: What each harness reaches now. The assertions check that a run does not fall below these, rather than demanding a perfect match - a suite that can never be green is a suite nobody reads, which is how a test that had stopped compiling went unread for several rounds. Raise a floor when something improves. A zero means the harness does not report its count yet.
_insn_remainder: The four cases of 9173 that do not match are two encodings that never start an instruction anywhere in the function map: E034 appears only as the low word of pea.l operands (capstone also misdecodes it - roxr.l #8 for what silicon runs as roxr.b d0,d4 - but no rox instruction exists at any boundary in the map, so no rule is wrong on a path that exists), and 0072 00F6 01A0 01A0 sits inside data at 0x276c. The harness executes every distinct encoding it finds, code or not; silicon obliged, the port's rules for junk stay unverified, and that is the right place to leave them.
_names: Readability, ratcheted. addressNamed is how many routines are still called fn_<address>, which says where a routine came from and nothing about what it does; namedParams is how many parameters are more than the register they arrived in. The bar in DELIVERY.md is addressNamed 0, with every name backed by recorded evidence rather than being merely plausible - a wrong name is worse than an address, and 0x9080 was confidently called creditCompare while it drains an unrelated ring buffer. Move these numbers whenever a session names something: the edit is the record that the work happened. romlab/distinguish.py prints, per routine, the evidence needed to name it. The thing it showed: a colliding name is a name for a region (touches the player structs), and what separates its members is one level finer - the d(An) displacement, i.e. which field. No player routine reaches the struct by absolute address, so the field offsets are the whole distinguishing fact. Name the structs first and the routines name themselves; the other way round recovers the same field map forty-two times.
_decompKnownWrong: Routines whose lift disagrees with the oracle, by address. One left of 1,161: 0xB032 writes 0x1B where the machine writes 0x05 at 0x3E0A69, one byte inside the board structures, on every trial - it walks the entity list at 0x3E1C84 and copies through a link frame, so the suspect is the frame or the list walk rather than an instruction rule. Anything not named here fails the harness.
_stepstate: Routines whose state the port reproduces at the address the frozen chip stopped on. It was 0 - a zero floor, which hid a regression that took this harness from 832 to 95 when its entry list was regenerated out from under its captures. The floor is the measurement now.
_writes: Writes the two dispatchers agree on before the first that differs, the minimum over all six input patterns. It is the whole recorded run at the default cap - 300,000 - on all six patterns. That is NOT identity, and calling it identity was wrong: the cap is the instrument's bound, not the game's. Raising it to 1,000,000 on `one player` (2026-07-31) puts the first differing work-RAM write at 582,338, at 0x3e3280, recompiled 0x504e against decompiled 0x4fb3, with 0x3e3274 also apart at 0x1d18 against 0x1d10 - counters, under counterStep, in the same 0x3E32xx block the original goal named. So the honest statement is: identical for the first 300,000 writes on every pattern, and diverging at 582,338 on the one pattern measured past that. It was 27,004 and then 39,666. Four faults in the lift accounted for the difference, and three were rules m68kts.py already had right and only decomp.py had dropped: bclr/bset/bchg set no flags at all, so a branch after a bit test read a stale one; absolute short addressing did not sign-extend, so $ffff.w came out 0x0000FFFF where the chip makes it 0xFFFFFFFF; and the shifts set neither N nor Z. The fourth was double bookkeeping, a routine running past the end of its own case range being ticked twice for one instruction. When the lift and the oracle disagree, diff the two emitters before theorising. Past the cap the runs still part - see _compose, which is the same seam - and WRITE_CAP raises it.
_compose: The frame at which the two dispatchers first differ, sampled once the machine is out of any handler. Measured 2026-07-31: frame 351, the same in five of six patterns, and the sixth (service switch) never differs. It is not a sampling artefact and not a lifting fault. entityListWalk opens with movem.l d2-d3/a2,-(a7), so the differing write is a register being saved, and the values are the low words of 0x55555555 and 0xFFFFFFFF - two of the four patterns fn_00430 cycles through while spinning until the frame handler sets 0x3E0802. The chip leaves that loop between instructions and the lifted code leaves it at a block head, which is the design decision that lets the sound driver's busy-wait terminate at all, so the two come out holding different patterns and a movem makes the difference visible. Whether that makes byte-identity through a whole game unreachable is NOT established - an earlier version of this note said it was, and that claim was withdrawn on 2026-07-31 after the alternatives were actually measured. What is established: both files already equalise the poll addresses; pacing the interrupt off poll count instead of cycles makes it worse, not better (first difference moves from frame 351 to frame 8, because the re-run discount leaves the runs a few polls out of phase and a frame-boundary snapshot is phase-sensitive); and replacing the discount's program-counter test with an exact interrupt-return test is worse again at the write level, five patterns identical against six. Corroboration found 2026-07-31 while naming: 0x130B0, the self-test driver, raises the interrupt mask to level 7 for its whole duration, so no frame interrupt arrives while it runs - and `service switch` is precisely the one pattern that never diverges here, where the other five all part at 351. A pattern with no interrupts shows no interrupt-timing seam. That is a natural experiment the pattern list already contained, and it is the strongest evidence yet that the divergence is the seam rather than a lifting fault. SAMPLE_POLLS compares state by program position rather than by frame boundary and is off by default. COMPOSE_ONLY='' COMPOSE_FRAMES=0 runs all six patterns at their full length in 67 seconds; the 1200-frame default is a cost bound from when that was unaffordable.
_draws: Pixels differing between the two runs at 600 frames: exactly 380 of 80,640, and every one of them is the deliberate wallCellSet change. Measured both ways on 2026-07-31 - regenerate without handedits.py and draws reports 'screens identical: 80640 pixels'; re-apply it and the 380 come back. The edit turns d3+0x4 into d3+0x0 and d3 is a tile index, so the changed rule draws a different wall tile: that is why work RAM stays byte-identical while these pixels do not, and why they sit only inside the wall glyphs at x 36..262, y 16..78. The assertion is now the exact count, not a floor - a floor would swallow a new fault as long as it hid under this footprint, and it would also pass if the change were silently lost. This replaces an earlier note claiming the run stopped before any wall was laid and blaming cycle drift; both were wrong.
_screens: What is actually on the screen, which is a different question from whether memory matched and had to be asked separately. compose MODIFIED now renders the visible 336x240 picture out of each run's final snapshot - playfield byte through the palette - reports the differing pixels' bounding box, and writes both crops as PNG so they can be looked at. Two faults in the instrument had to go first: it digested the raw playfield rather than the picture, and `shot` was only populated during replay, so the first version compared two blank screens and reported 'no difference' for everything. Measured 2026-07-31 at 900 frames. attract and the long idle run differ only inside the wall glyphs at x 36..262, y 16..78 - that is the deliberate wallCellSet change and nothing else. The three-station and service-switch patterns lay no wall, so there is nothing to see. But `one player` and `two players` differ in 4608 pixels in a box at x 12..331, y 96..111, a full-width sixteen-pixel strip that is NOT wall: it is the station select banner, and the PNGs show both runs drawing the same words BLUE RED ORANGE with different panel colours - the recompiled run colours each panel to match its word, the decompiled run paints all three green. Reverting the hand edit reproduces the same 4608 pixels in the same box, so this is entirely independent of wallCellSet, and draws.test never saw it because draws.test only runs attract. Traced 2026-07-31 with writes.test: palette writes are identical (7090 of them, W_LO=0x3c0000 W_HI=0x3c1000), so it is not the palette - it is the playfield bytes. Windowed on the strip itself (W_LO=0x20c000 W_HI=0x20e000) the two part at write 26216 of 31528, at 0x20c00c, recompiled 0x9b against decompiled 0x8b: one bit, 0x10, and the high nibble of a colour index is the palette bank. The stack names graphicsDecompressor under decompressOneEightPixelColumnFrom1, and the lift shows the stored byte is (d3.w >>> 4) + d2.w where d2 is the colour base the caller passes in as arg8. graphicsDecompressor is not in decompKnownWrong - it verifies clean against the oracle on random states - so the suspect is upstream: a caller selecting a different palette bank for the banner panels. That is the next thing to chase and it is the first genuinely wrong thing found on screen rather than in memory. TRACED FURTHER 2026-07-31 with the new ROM-stack walk. The caller is fn_036a2, which pushes d1 as the decompressor's arg8, and builds it as d1 = (load8(ptr) << 4) + load16(dst - 2). The stack shows that product as 0x90 against 0x80, so load8(ptr) is 9 in the recompiled run and 8 in the decompiled one - and ptr itself differs, 0x3f179 against 0x3ef80. The two runs are reading the colour out of different records, so this is not a lifting fault in the drawing path at all: it is downstream of a work-RAM state difference, and work RAM does diverge on this pattern at write 582,338 (see _writes). The banner is the first place that difference becomes visible, which makes it the symptom and the counters at 0x3e327x the disease.
_romstack: How to find the caller, which the JavaScript stack cannot tell you. Both dispatchers are trampolines - a routine calls another by returning to the loop with a new program counter - so ROM call depth is not JS call depth and writes.test's `stack:` line bottoms out in `call <- callDecompiled <- callRom` no matter how deep the ROM is. The chain is on the machine's own stack and in the same form in both runs, so writes.test now walks it at the divergence and prints both. It reads longwords at every two bytes, so consecutive entries overlap and half of what it prints is a shifted duplicate of its neighbour - read every other one, and check any address against facts.json before believing it. It paid for itself immediately: on the banner-colour fault it showed 0x11f1e (the return into the decompressor wrapper), then the pushed arguments, of which one read 0x90 in the recompiled run and 0x80 in the decompiled - the colour bank, the whole bug, sitting in plain sight on the stack.
_3e32xx: What the 0x3E3200-0x3E32C0 window actually is, because the name it was given was wrong. Windowed there on `one player` (2026-07-31) the runs part at write 23,967 of 252,189, and the writes descend - 0x3e3280, then 0x3e327e, then 0x3e327c - with a7 sitting at 0x3e327e and a6 at 0x3e32c2. That is the machine stack, not a sound sequencer's state: these are pushes, and what differs is the contents of registers being spilled. The ROM stack walk prints the same chain for both runs, longword for longword, so the call path is identical and only the values are apart: 0x504e against 0x4fb3 at 0x3e3280, and 0x1d18 against 0x1d10 at 0x3e3274, under counterStep into extractsOwnerBitsCellByte. Same shape as the known seam at fn_00430 - a register spill exposing a value the two dispatchers hold differently - but here it is NOT self-evidently the seam, because it propagates: this is the same divergence that, further on, hands fn_036a2 a different record pointer and paints the station banner green (see _screens). So the open question is precisely whether 0x504e/0x4fb3 is interrupt-timing residue or a real counter, and that is what to answer next. First discriminator run 2026-07-31: WAIT_SKIP=1 leaves the divergence at exactly write 23,967, unmoved. So this is NOT the fn_00430 spin loop that accounts for the frame-351 seam - excluding that loop entirely changes nothing here. Taken with the identical ROM stacks, that means the two runs walk the same code path with the same call chain and hold different values in registers, for a reason not yet identified and not the known seam. Worth noting but not yet meaningful: 0x504e - 0x4fb3 is 0x9B, 155, and the cycle clocks are 142 apart at the first write in this window, which is the right order of magnitude for a cycle-derived quantity - but the game cannot read a cycle counter, so if that resemblance is real it has to arrive through something paced by interrupts. SETTLED 2026-07-31, and it changes the answer to the whole equivalence question. IRQ_PHASE shifts the first interrupt; run the same window at phase 0 and phase 1511 and both dispatchers return byte-identical values - recompiled 0x504e at both, decompiled 0x4fb3 at both. Residue of where an interrupt landed moves when the phase moves. This does not. So 0x504e is a quantity the game computed and 0x4fb3 is the decompilation computing it wrongly: a REAL lifting fault, not a seam, and therefore fixable. That matters beyond this one value, because the standing assumption - that what is left between the two runs is the interrupt seam - is now known to be false for at least this divergence, and byte-identity through a full game is back on the table rather than argued away. The resemblance to the cycle gap (0x9B against 142) was a coincidence and is now retracted. What is known: identical ROM call chains, identical under WAIT_SKIP, identical under phase shift, one wrong number under counterStep into extractsOwnerBitsCellByte, and it propagates all the way to a green station banner. What is not: which routine computes it. decomp.test proves routines one at a time against the oracle and passes, so either the fault needs a state the random harness never builds - the movep lesson - or it is a composition effect across routines.
